description: Labeled eval set for testing RAG retrieval quality. For each entry, run the question through your retrieval step and check whether the retrieved chunk(s) actually contain the source_snippet — that's your hit-rate/Precision@k signal. Compare the LLM's generated answer to expected_answer for faithfulness.
usage_notes: difficulty='exact': answer is a direct definition lookup — should be easy to retrieve correctly.
difficulty='paraphrase': question is worded differently than the source text — tests whether your embedding model captures semantic similarity, not just keyword overlap.
difficulty='synthesis': answer requires combining info from more than one sentence/section — tests whether your chunk size/overlap preserves enough context, and whether top-k > 1 is needed.

eval_pairs.question: What is the formal definition of a directed graph?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: A directed graph (digraph) is a pair G = (V, A) where V is a set of vertices and A is a subset of V x V, a set of directed edges (arcs).
eval_pairs.source_snippet: a directed graph or (digraph) is a pair G = (V, A) where V is a set of vertices (or nodes), and A ⊆ V × V is a set of directed edges (or arcs)

eval_pairs.question: How is an undirected graph formally defined, and why can't it have self loops?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: An undirected graph is a pair G = (V, E) where E is a set of unordered pairs {u, v}. Self loops aren't possible because {v, v} = {v}, which isn't a valid element of the edge set (defined as unordered pairs of two distinct vertices).
eval_pairs.source_snippet: an undirected graph is a pair G = (V, E) where V is a set of vertices... E ⊆ (V choose 2) is a set of edges... an undirected graph cannot have self loops since {v, v} = {v} not in (V choose 2)

eval_pairs.question: Why are graphs considered more expressive than trees for representing relationships?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Trees cannot have cycles or multiple paths between two nodes, while graphs can, making graphs more general and expressive.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: Graphs are more interesting than other abstractions such as tree... because graphs are more expressive. For example, in a tree, tree cannot be cycles, and multiple paths between two nodes.

eval_pairs.question: What's the difference between an in-neighbor and an out-neighbor in a directed graph?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: For a directed graph, u is an in-neighbor of v if (u, v) is an edge, and u is an out-neighbor of v if (v, u) is an edge.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: For a directed graph a vertex u is an in-neighbor of a vertex v if (u, v) ∈ E and an out-neighbor if (v, u) ∈ E

eval_pairs.question: How is the degree of a vertex defined, and how does it differ for directed graphs?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: The degree of a vertex is the size of its neighborhood. For directed graphs, this splits into in-degree (size of in-neighborhood) and out-degree (size of out-neighborhood).
eval_pairs.source_snippet: The degree dG(v) of a vertex v ∈ V in a graph G = (V, E) is the size of the neighborhood |NG(v)|. For directed graphs we use in-degree... and out-degree

eval_pairs.question: What separates a path from a simple path?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: A path is a sequence of adjacent vertices (repeats allowed). A simple path has no repeated vertices.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: A path in a graph is a sequence of adjacent vertices... A simple path is a path with no repeated vertices.

eval_pairs.question: Why must an undirected cycle have a minimum length of three?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: The document states this as a requirement for simple cycles in undirected graphs but poses it as an exercise for the reader to reason through rather than stating the reason directly — worth flagging as a question the model shouldn't fabricate an answer for if that section isn't retrieved.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: has no repeated vertices other than the first and last, and has length at least three... Why is important in a undirected graph to require that a cycle has length at least three?

eval_pairs.question: What makes a graph a forest versus a tree?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: An undirected graph with no cycles is a forest; if it's also connected, it's a tree.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: An undirected graph with no cycles is a forest and if it is connected it is called a tree.

eval_pairs.question: What's a DAG?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no cycles.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: A directed graph with no cycles is a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

eval_pairs.question: How are distance and diameter defined for a graph?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Distance from u to v is the shortest path length between them. Diameter is the maximum shortest path length over all pairs of vertices in the graph.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: The distance δG(u, v) from a vertex u to a vertex v... is the shortest path... The diameter of a graph is the maximum shortest path length over all pairs of vertices

eval_pairs.question: When is a graph considered sparse versus dense?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: A graph is informally sparse if the number of edges m is much less than n^2 (n being the number of vertices), and dense otherwise.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: We informally say that a graph is sparse if m ≪ n^2 and dense otherwise.

eval_pairs.question: Give three real-world applications of graphs mentioned in the text.
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Examples include social network graphs (e.g. Twitter follower graphs), transportation networks (road/public transit systems), and protein-protein interaction graphs.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: Social network graphs... Transportation networks... Protein-protein interactions graphs

eval_pairs.question: In document link graphs, what do vertices and edges represent?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Each web page is a vertex, and each hyperlink is a directed edge.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: the link graph of the web, where each web page is a vertex, and each hyperlink a directed edge

eval_pairs.question: What is the main drawback of representing a graph with an adjacency matrix?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Its space demand is Theta(n^2), which is wasteful for sparse graphs that have far fewer edges than n^2.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: The main problem with adjacency matrices is their space demand of Θ(n^2). Graphs are often sparse, with far fewer edges than Θ(n^2).

eval_pairs.question: Why are adjacency lists poorly suited for parallel algorithms?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Because traversing the neighbors of a vertex in an adjacency list requires sequentially walking a linked list.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: Adjacency lists are not well suited for parallelism since the lists require that we traverse the neighbors of a vertex sequentially.

eval_pairs.question: How does an adjacency array differ structurally from an adjacency list?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: An adjacency array stores all vertices' neighbors consecutively in one array, plus a separate index array marking where each vertex's neighbor block starts — rather than using pointers to linked lists like an adjacency list.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: an adjacency array keeps the neighbors of all vertices, one after another, in an array adj; and separately, keeps an array of indices

eval_pairs.question: What is an edge list?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: A list of vertex pairs (i, j) that are in the edge set E.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: Edge list. A list of pairs (i, j) ∈ E.

eval_pairs.question: Why does the book use edge sets and adjacency tables instead of low-level structures like arrays or linked lists?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: To keep the representation abstract (based on sets and tables) so parallel operations apply more easily, and so vertices don't need to be restricted to labels 1 through n.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: we take a more abstract view of the representation of graphs... This makes it easier to apply parallel operations to the graphs. It also allows us to use arbitrary sets of vertices

eval_pairs.question: Why are edge sets inefficient for finding all neighbors of a vertex, even though they're efficient for checking if a specific edge exists?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: Checking if an edge exists is a direct lookup (O(log n) work), but finding all neighbors of a vertex requires filtering the entire edge set for matches, which takes Theta(m) work.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: edge sets are efficient for finding, inserting, or deleting an edge, they are not efficient if we want to identify the neighbors of a vertex... requires a filter... For m edges this requires Θ(m) work

eval_pairs.question: What is the work and span cost of accessing the neighbors of a vertex using an adjacency table?
eval_pairs.expected_answer: O(log n) work and O(log n) span, since it's just a lookup in the table.
eval_pairs.source_snippet: accessing the out neighbors of a vertex v is cheap since it just requires a lookup in the table. Assuming the tree cost model for tables, this can be done in O(log n) work and span.
